questions.question: Which of these statements about classes and objects are true?
options: A class is a template; an object is a concrete instance of it
Several objects can be created from a single class
A class is an instance of an object
A class can only be instantiated once
Defining a class automatically creates one object
A class and an object are two words for the same thing
questions.explanation: The class describes attributes and behaviour; each object is a separate concrete entity built from that template.

questions.question: What does type(dog).__name__ return?
questions.explanation: type(obj) gives the class, and __name__ gives its name as a string. Useful inside a generic __repr__.

questions.question: Which statements about class attributes and instance attributes are true?
options: A class attribute is shared by every instance of the class
An attribute assigned in __init__ belongs to that instance only
Instance attributes are shared by every instance
A class attribute is copied into each new instance
A class cannot define attributes outside __init__
Class attributes may only hold integers
questions.explanation: A mutable class attribute is a classic trap: appending to it from one instance is visible from all the others.

questions.question: What is the value of b.total?
questions.code:
class Counter:
    total = 0

    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0

a = Counter()
b = Counter()
Counter.total = 5
questions.explanation: total is a class attribute: changing it on the class is immediately visible from every instance that has not shadowed it.

questions.question: Person.__init__ takes name and age. Which expression creates an instance?
questions.explanation: Python has no new keyword: calling the class runs __init__, and self is passed automatically.

questions.question: Given class Dog(Animal) and d = Dog(), which statements are true?
questions.explanation: isinstance takes inheritance into account, type() does not: type(d) is exactly Dog, never Animal.

questions.question: Which statements about the OOP concepts seen in the course are true?
options: Inheritance lets a class reuse the attributes and methods of another class
Polymorphism means the same method name can behave differently depending on the class
Encapsulation means a class can inherit from several parents
Abstraction means bundling data and methods together
Composition means overriding a method of the parent
questions.explanation: Encapsulation bundles data and code, abstraction hides details, composition stores an object inside another.

questions.question: What is encapsulation?
options: Bundling data and the methods that operate on it inside a single class
Creating a new class from an existing one
Using the same method name with different behaviours
Hiding details and exposing only the essentials
Storing an object as an attribute of another object
questions.explanation: The other options describe inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, composition and operator overloading.

questions.question: When is __init__ called?
options: Automatically, every time the class is instantiated
Only when you call it explicitly
Once per class, when the class is defined
Every time a method of the object is called
Only if the class declares attributes
questions.explanation: __init__ initialises the object that has just been created; it can take parameters to set different attributes.

questions.question: What must __init__ return?
options: Nothing: returning anything other than None raises a TypeError
questions.explanation: The object is built before __init__ runs. __init__ only initialises it, which is why it must not return a value.

questions.question: Which statements about self are true?
options: It refers to the instance on which the method is called
The first parameter of an instance method receives the instance, whatever its name
It is a reserved Python keyword
You must pass it explicitly when calling the method
It refers to the class, not to the instance
It may be omitted from any method
questions.explanation: self is a convention, not a keyword: only its position matters. Python passes the instance automatically.

questions.question: What does print(cat.voice) display?
questions.explanation: The constructor stored the argument in the attribute self.voice, which is then read on the instance.

questions.question: Person defines def greet(self). For p = Person("Alice", 30), which calls work?
questions.explanation: p.greet() is shorthand for Person.greet(p): the instance is passed as the first argument either way.

questions.question: Which calls are valid?
questions.explanation: start has a default value, so it becomes optional. self is never passed by hand.

questions.question: A child class defines __init__ but never calls super().__init__(). What happens?
options: The attributes created by the parent constructor are missing from the instance
Python calls the parent constructor automatically anyway
A TypeError is raised at instantiation
The child class can no longer define attributes
The methods inherited from the parent become unavailable
Nothing changes: super() is purely cosmetic
questions.explanation: Defining __init__ in the child completely replaces the parent's. The failure shows up later, as an AttributeError.

questions.question: By default, member variables and methods of a Python class are:
questions.explanation: Python has no access keywords: everything is public, and underscores only express an intention.

questions.question: How do you mark a member as protected?
options: Prefix its name with a single underscore: _value
Prefix its name with two underscores: __value
questions.explanation: A single underscore says "internal use". Two underscores mean private and trigger name mangling.

questions.question: How do you mark a member as private?
options: Prefix its name with at least two underscores: __value
Prefix its name with a single underscore: _value
Declare it as a class attribute
Define it after all the methods
questions.explanation: Two leading underscores make Python rename the attribute, which hides it from ordinary outside access.

questions.question: Which statements are true?
options: The attribute no longer exists on the object
Python forbids any access to the value
A private attribute cannot be read even from inside the class
questions.explanation: Name mangling renames __varPrivate into _Test__varPrivate. The value is hidden, not protected.

questions.question: What does the single underscore in _balance actually enforce?
options: Nothing technically: it is a convention telling other developers not to touch it
Python blocks any access from outside the class
It makes the attribute shared by all instances
It prints a warning at runtime
questions.explanation: Encapsulation in Python rests on discipline, not on the language. _balance stays perfectly reachable.

questions.question: Which statements about name mangling are true?
options: It makes accidental access from outside unlikely, but not impossible
It encrypts the value of the attribute
It applies to names with a single leading underscore
It deletes the attribute once __init__ returns
It turns the attribute into a class attribute
questions.explanation: Mangling is a renaming, nothing more. Its real purpose is to avoid name clashes between a class and its subclasses.

questions.question: In class Dog(Animal):, which statements are true?
options: Dog is the subclass (child) and Animal the superclass (parent)
Dog inherits the attributes and methods of Animal
Dog must redefine every method of Animal
Animal is an instance of Dog
questions.explanation: The child reuses everything the parent offers, and is free to add to it or to override parts of it.

questions.question: What is method overriding?
options: A subclass redefines a method that already exists in its parent
Two methods with the same name but different parameters in one class
Calling a parent method from the child
Creating several instances of the same class
questions.explanation: Overriding is what makes polymorphism possible: the same call, a different implementation per class.

questions.question: What does super().__init__(name) do inside a child constructor?
options: It calls the constructor of the parent class
It creates a separate instance of the parent class
It copies the parent class into the child
It erases the attributes of the child
It returns the parent class object
It is only needed when the child defines no attribute
questions.explanation: Without it, the initialisation written in the parent simply never runs.

questions.question: Which expressions are valid?
questions.explanation: name and breed are instance attributes: they live on d, not on the classes, so Dog.name raises an AttributeError.

questions.question: What does bird.speak(3) return?
questions.explanation: Bird overrides speak and adds an optional parameter. Multiplying a string repeats it.

questions.question: A subclass can:
options: Override a method of its parent
Prevent the parent from being instantiated
Only use the parent methods unchanged
questions.explanation: Inheritance is additive: the child starts from everything the parent has, then extends or replaces what it needs.

questions.question: In the course example, what does def speak(self): pass express in the parent class?
options: A default behaviour that subclasses are expected to override
That the method cannot be overridden
That calling the method raises an error
That the method returns an empty string
That the class cannot be instantiated
questions.explanation: pass silently returns None, so a forgotten override goes unnoticed. Raising NotImplementedError makes it explicit.

questions.question: From inside Dog.speak, which expressions call the parent implementation?
questions.explanation: self.speak() would call the child's own version again, which loops forever.

questions.question: What does polymorphism allow?
options: Calling the same method name on different classes and getting the behaviour of each
Defining several classes with the same name
Creating an object without a class
Having two attributes with the same name in one object
Hiding an attribute from outside the class
Converting one class into another automatically
questions.explanation: The calling code manipulates objects that share a parent without needing to know their exact type.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: Bird.speak uses its default repeat=2. Each object runs the version defined in its own class.

questions.question: In for animal in animals: print(animal.speak()), how does Python choose which speak to run?
options: From the actual class of the object, at runtime
From the type declared for the list
From the first class defined in the file
From the alphabetical order of the class names
questions.explanation: Attribute lookup starts on the object's own class, then walks up the inheritance chain.

questions.question: Which of these are examples of polymorphism?
options: Two subclasses overriding the same parent method differently
len() working on a string, a list and a dictionary
Two attributes holding the same value
A class defining a private attribute
Storing an object as an attribute of another object
questions.explanation: len() delegates to each type's own __len__: one name, many implementations.

questions.question: Why does sum(shape.computeArea() for shape in shapes) work on a list mixing rectangles, circles and squares?
options: Because every shape class implements computeArea(), each in its own way
Because Python converts every shape into a Rectangle
Because sum() knows how to compute an area
Because all the shapes have the same area
Because the list is sorted by type
Because computeArea() is defined only in the parent class
questions.explanation: This is the practical payoff of polymorphism: one line of calling code, one implementation per class.

questions.question: What is composition?
options: An attribute of an object is itself an object of another class
A class inherits from two parents
A method is redefined in a subclass
Several objects share a class attribute
questions.explanation: A BankAccount holding a list of Transaction objects is composition.

questions.question: Which statements pair the relationship with the right name?
questions.explanation: A Square is a Rectangle (inheritance); an account has transactions (composition).

questions.question: What is abstraction?
options: Hiding implementation details and exposing only what is essential
Bundling data and methods inside one class
Reusing the methods of another class
Using one method name for several behaviours
Storing an object inside another object
questions.explanation: The user of a BankAccount calls deposit() without knowing how the history is stored.

questions.question: How can you force a subclass to provide its own implementation of a method?
options: Raise NotImplementedError in the parent implementation
Decorate it with @abstractmethod in a class inheriting from ABC
Write the abstract keyword before def
Leave the method out of the parent entirely
Prefix the method name with two underscores
Declare the parent class as private
questions.explanation: NotImplementedError fails when the method is called; @abstractmethod fails earlier, at instantiation.

questions.question: In a UML class diagram, what does an italic class or method name mean?
options: It is inherited from another class
questions.explanation: In the exercise, BankAccount and its withdrawal method are italic: the class is not meant to be instantiated directly.

questions.question: Which magic method overloads the + operator?
questions.explanation: __iadd__ handles +=, and __radd__ the case where the object is on the right-hand side.

questions.question: Which magic method overloads the / operator?
questions.explanation: __floordiv__ is for //. The name __div__ belonged to Python 2 and no longer exists.

questions.question: Which operator / magic method pairs are correct?
questions.explanation: The right names are __mul__ for *, __sub__ for -, __truediv__ for / and __floordiv__ for //.

questions.question: What does this program display?
questions.explanation: __add__ builds and returns a new Vector, and __repr__ controls how print displays it.

questions.question: Vector defines __mul__(self, scalar) only. Which expressions work?
questions.explanation: 3 * v would need __rmul__, the reflected version used when the object is the right-hand operand.

questions.question: A class defines no __add__ at all. What does obj1 + obj2 do?
options: It raises a TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +
It adds the objects attribute by attribute
questions.explanation: Python never guesses what + should mean on your objects: without __add__ the operation is simply unsupported.

questions.question: What does __add__ have to return to allow chained expressions such as v1 + v2 + v3?
options: A new object of the same class
questions.explanation: Returning a new instance keeps the operands untouched and lets the result take part in another operation.

questions.question: Which magic method overloads the < operator?
questions.explanation: __le__ is for <=, __gt__ for > and __ge__ for >=.

questions.question: Which operator / magic method pairs are correct?
questions.explanation: The remaining correct names are __eq__ for ==, __ne__ for != and __gt__ for >.

questions.question: A class defines __eq__ but not __ne__. What does a != b do?
options: Python derives the result automatically from __eq__
questions.explanation: Since Python 3, != is the negation of == unless __ne__ is explicitly defined.

questions.question: A class defines __eq__ but no __hash__. Which statements are true?
options: They can no longer be used as dictionary keys or set elements
The class can no longer be instantiated
questions.explanation: Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None. Two equal objects must have the same hash, so Python refuses to guess.

questions.question: A class defines __lt__ only. Which comparisons between two of its instances work?
questions.explanation: For a > b Python first tries a.__gt__(b); as it is missing, it falls back to the reflected call b.__lt__(a).

questions.question: To compare two fractions a/b and c/d, why prefer a*d < c*b over a/b < c/d?
options: It stays in integer arithmetic and avoids floating-point rounding
It is the only syntax Python accepts
Because / is not defined on integers
Because the cross product is always positive
Because it also works when a denominator is zero
questions.explanation: This holds as long as the denominators are positive, which is why the constructor normalises the sign.

questions.question: Which magic method does the += operator use?
questions.explanation: The i stands for in place: __iadd__, __isub__, __imul__, and so on.

questions.question: A class defines __add__ but not __iadd__. What does obj += other do?
options: Python falls back to __add__ and rebinds the name to the new object
questions.explanation: obj += other becomes obj = obj + other, so obj ends up pointing at a brand new object.

questions.question: Which operator / magic method pairs are correct?
questions.explanation: The right names are __isub__, __itruediv__, __imod__ and __ipow__.

questions.question: What is the point of defining __iadd__ rather than relying on __add__?
options: To modify the object in place instead of building a new one
To allow the object on the right-hand side
questions.explanation: This is what makes list += cheap: it extends the existing list instead of rebuilding one.

questions.question: What does print(obj) use?
options: __str__, falling back to __repr__ when __str__ is not defined
questions.explanation: Defining only __repr__ is therefore enough to control both print(obj) and repr(obj).

questions.question: A class defines __repr__ but not __str__. Which statements are true?
options: str(obj) returns the default <object at 0x...> form
questions.explanation: __str__ defaults to __repr__, which is why a single __repr__ covers every display path.

questions.question: What does this display?
options: A line such as <__main__.Point object at 0x000...>
questions.explanation: Without __repr__ or __str__, Python falls back to the default representation: class name and memory address.

questions.question: What should __repr__ ideally return?
options: An unambiguous representation, ideally one that could recreate the object
The memory address of the object
The list of the class methods
The name of the class only
A boolean telling whether the object is valid
questions.explanation: Vector(5, 7, 9) is a good __repr__: read it and you know exactly how to rebuild the object.

questions.question: In the exercise, CheckingAccount and SavingsAccount both define withdrawal(). This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Each account overrides withdrawal, and the same call then behaves differently depending on the account type.

questions.question: Why store the balance as _balance and expose a get_balance() accessor?
options: So that every change goes through deposit()/withdrawal() and lands in the transaction history
Because Python forbids public numeric attributes
To speed up the computation of the balance
Because the UML diagram requires an underscore
questions.explanation: This is encapsulation in practice: control the writes and no operation can escape the history.

questions.question: What should Fractional(42, 0) do?
options: Raise an exception, because a zero denominator has no meaning
Store the values as they are and fail later
questions.explanation: Failing at construction reports the problem where it is caused, rather than far away from it.

questions.question: Why reduce a fraction inside __init__?
options: So that Fractional(2, 4) and Fractional(1, 2) compare as equal
So that the numerator is always positive
Because Python requires a denominator below 100
So that __repr__ can display a float
To make the division operator faster
questions.explanation: Without reduction, an __eq__ comparing numerator and denominator would consider 2/4 and 1/2 different.

questions.question: In the shapes exercise, why write class Square(Rectangle) rather than class Square(Shape)?
options: Because a square is a rectangle, so it reuses width, height and computeArea()
Because Shape cannot have more than two subclasses
Because a square has no area
Because Python forbids inheriting directly from Shape
Because computeArea() is defined only in Rectangle
questions.explanation: Square only has to pass the same value as width and height to super().__init__().

questions.question: In the bank exercise, which design choices does the transaction history rely on?
options: Composition: the account holds a list of Transaction objects
Encapsulation: only deposit() and withdrawal() may change the balance
Name mangling: the history is stored as __history
questions.explanation: The history is an attribute made of objects of another class, and it stays reliable only because writes are funnelled.
